newsitem.title: JAPAN: WEEK AHEAD - Tokyo stocks seen suffering further.
newsitem.headline: WEEK AHEAD - Tokyo stocks seen suffering further.

text.p: Tokyo stocks are likely to fall further in the week ahead on spreading skepticism about the government's handling of the economy.

The key Nikkei share average posted a moderate rebound on Friday, helped by an overnight spurt on Wall Street, to break its three-day losing streak. It closed at 19,690.46, down 650.93 points from its closing on December 13.
Brokers predicted that the rebound would be temporary and the bottom vulnerable.

"The Nikkei posted a mild recovery just because of the New York rally but I still expect it to head downwards next week or in January," Haruyoshi Mabuchi, chief strategist at Nikko Research Center, said on Friday.
He said the bearishness reflected market concern about government economic policies, now geared more to belt-tightening and deficit-cutting than to growth.
"I think it is very possible that the Nikkei will dip to 19,000 by the end of the year," said Tetsuya Ishijima, chief strategist at Okasan Securities Co Ltd.
On Friday Japan's cabinet approved a tighter state budget for the next fiscal year from April 1, 1997, in an effort to put its debt-ridden finances in order.
"The government decided to end special income tax cuts and raise the consumption tax. This made us worry about whether the government is really trying to support the economy," Mabuchi said.
The market was dismayed by confirmation on Wednesday that the government planned to scrap special income tax cuts that had previously been granted to help the economy recover.

"We understand that the government needs to balance its budget. But at the same time, the market wants to see something more to prop up the economy, like specific deregulatory measures," said Okasan's Ishijima.
Analysts said the market grew more despondent after the Nikkei fell below the key 20,000 level on Thursday.
Some brokers said public pension funds put in buying orders on Friday, especially before the market closed, aiming to lift the index.
Some added that they were worried that the hostage crisis at the Japanese ambassador's residence in Peru might deflect the government's attention from financial matters.
